newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia declares war on rabbit pests.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia declares war on rabbit pests.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday declared biological warfare on an estimated 200 million rabbits.

Farmers blame the creatures -- imported by a British hunting fan in the 19th century -- for causing hundreds of millions of dollars of damage to crops and driving indigenous animals and plants to the verge of exinction.

The rabbit population received its first dose of the deadly calicivirus disease near the outback town of Wagga Wagga, where New South Wales Agriculture Minister Richard Amery released 20 infected rabbits into the wild.
"It's probably the best news the environment has had in 20 years," said Mick Keogh, a farmers' representative.
Government officials say the disease will eventually be released at 280 sites in all of Australia's states and territories, although some wild rabbits have already been accidentally infected.
Supporters of the move hope the disease will eradicate up to 80 percent of the rabbit populaton within two years. Rabbits currently outnumber humans in Australia by around 10 to one.
Amery said rabbits were responsible for the decline of many native Australian animals such as wombats and bilbies as well as native plants pushed to extinction,
Others criticised the action as premature, however, saying the virus could pose dangers outside the rabbit world.

"We question the assurances of scientists and regulators that the virus will not infect native or domestic animals and cannot cross the humans," Bob Phelps, an Australian Conservation Foundation spokesman said.
"The virus crossed into rabbits and it may only be a matter of time before it moves on," he said.
Doctor Lyn Hinds of Australia's Vertebrate Biocontrol Centre, which is involved in government pest control activitis, said she could not rule out the disease spreading but the odds were against it.
"Noone can categorically say that it will never jump over into another species, but the evidence to date shows that it seems to be highly specific to the rabbit," Hinds said.

Australia also is battling to reduce its population of kangaroos, estimated to be in the millions, Hinds said. One long-term project under consideration was to use anti-fertility drugs to control the country's most famous native creature.
